nameStory: Quince rust gets its name from the telltale rusty orange spots it creates on quince trees and other members of the rose family. The 'rust' refers to the distinctive reddish-brown color of the fungal spores, which look remarkably like iron rust staining the leaves and fruit of infected plants.
description: Quince rust is a fascinating fungus that needs two completely different types of trees to survive - it can't complete its life cycle on just one host. On quince, apple, and hawthorn trees, it appears as bright orange or rust-colored spots on leaves and sometimes fruit. On its evergreen hosts like eastern red cedar and other junipers, it forms small, brownish galls or swellings on branches. This fungus is actually quite common but often goes unnoticed because people don't realize the orange spots on their fruit trees are connected to those little bumps on nearby cedar trees.

idTips.label: Orange leaf spots
idTips.description: Bright orange to rust-colored circular spots on the upper surface of leaves, often with a slightly raised texture that feels bumpy to the touch

idTips.label: Cedar galls
idTips.description: Small, hard, brownish rounded swellings on juniper or cedar branches that feel woody and solid when pressed

idTips.label: Fruit infections
idTips.description: Orange spots or patches on quince, apple, or hawthorn fruit that may feel slightly sunken or rough compared to healthy skin

idTips.label: Host plant requirement
idTips.description: Always found where both rose family trees (apple, quince, hawthorn) and junipers/cedars grow within a few hundred yards of each other

idTips.label: Leaf yellowing
idTips.description: Infected leaves may turn yellow around the rust spots and feel slightly thicker or more brittle than healthy leaves

habitat: You'll find quince rust in areas where ornamental or wild apple, quince, or hawthorn trees grow near eastern red cedars or other juniper species. This includes suburban neighborhoods with mixed landscaping, old farmsteads with fruit trees, forest edges, and abandoned orchards. The fungus requires both host types to be relatively close together, typically within a few hundred yards.

seasonality.spring: Orange spots begin appearing on new leaves of rose family trees. Cedar galls may release bright orange, gelatinous spore masses during wet weather.
seasonality.summer: Rust spots are most visible and numerous on leaves and developing fruit. The infections are often at their most colorful and obvious during hot, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Infected leaves may drop early, and fruit infections become more apparent. Cedar galls continue developing on evergreen hosts.
seasonality.winter: Cedar galls remain visible as small brown bumps on juniper branches, while deciduous host trees show no visible signs of infection.

funFact: This sneaky fungus is like a botanical shapeshifter - it produces completely different spore types on its two host plants, and for years scientists thought they were looking at two separate species until they discovered the fungus was living a secret double life!
confusionNotes: Quince rust is easily confused with cedar-apple rust, which causes very similar orange spots. The key difference is in the fruit affected - quince rust primarily targets quince trees (and sometimes apples), while cedar-apple rust mainly goes after apples and crabapples. Memory trick: 'Quince rust loves quinces best.'
contextualKnowledge: Many gardeners don't realize that removing either the fruit trees OR the nearby cedars and junipers can help control this rust disease, since the fungus absolutely requires both host types to survive. This is why you'll sometimes see recommendations to avoid planting these tree types near each other.
compareHints: Quince rust is most similar to cedar-apple rust, but quince rust tends to create more numerous, smaller spots and shows a stronger preference for quince trees specifically. Cedar-hawthorn rust forms larger, more irregular patches and primarily targets hawthorn trees. Quince rust's cedar galls are typically smaller and less conspicuous than the large, golf ball-sized galls produced by cedar-apple rust.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cedar-apple rust creates the most dramatically gelatinous orange masses compared to its relatives.
Pear rust differs from cedar-apple rust by targeting pears instead of apples and having smaller, more numerous orange spots rather than large yellow-orange blotches.
